subject: Applying fitted detection function to new data?

messages.author: 5b4763d3a422c983
messages.subject: Applying fitted detection function to new data?
parts:
Hello all,

We're using distance sampling to estimate abundance of moose, with data gathered along line transects during aerial surveys. The population we're working with is small and sparsely distributed across a large geographic area. In previous years, aerial surveys generated too few detections to accurately model a detection function, so during this year's surveys we focused exclusively on acquiring enough detections to get a precise estimate of detection, including covariates, with the hopes of using this function as a robust model for application to future surveys. Fortunately, we acquired enough detections this year to test several covariates and ended up with a fitted detection function with a covariate on habitat type and a low coefficient of variation.

Is there a way, using Distance, to apply this detection function to new data? So, for example, if we wanted to estimate abundance in 2016 using last year's survey data, is there a way to use our fitted detection function from this year with last year's data? We have no reason to suspect that detection probabilities would change between years. We're using the most recent version of Distance in R.

Any help would be much appreciated.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Applying fitted detection function to new data? incomplete answer
parts:
Rachel

I direct you to a section in the Users Guide of the graphic interface version of Distance in Chapter 10 "Mark-recapture distance sampling" where there is a description of re-using a detection function for a different dataset (section entitled "Using a Previously Fitted Detection Function to Estimate Density in MRDS").  Unfortunately, I would not recommend this as a solution for you, because you would need to organise and enter your data as if it were double-observer data, even though it was collected (I presume) from a single observer platform.

Beyond the mechanics of getting the software to do your bidding, I encourage you to re-think your intended analysis.

IF (I repeat IF) you are confident the relationship of detectability and habitat is constant over time, you will likely need to defend that assumption. 

You may be able to compute what you desire in R using a combination of calls to ds() in the Distance package followed by calls to predict() in the mrds() package; but I am in over my head at that point.  Perhaps others have more thorough solutions.

messages.author: 208520df5a1c57c2
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Applying fitted detection function to new data? incomplete answer
parts:
I won't comment on the advisability or otherwise of using a multi-year detection function, but there is an easy work-around I think:

Put all detections from previous years in a separate stratum with 0 surface area. That way these detections are used in the detection function but do not contribute to the final abundance estimate. 

Of course your "new" data will also be included in the detection function, but I assume you would want that. You would probably also want to use the function at the stratum level in this case.

Daniel Pike.

You might want to consider using mcds and include year as a factor.  (You can extract AIC for the mcds model and for the model without year, and compare them, to assess whether detectability changes across years.)

 

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Applying fitted detection function to new data? incomplete answer
parts:
Eric, Daniel, and Steve,

Thank you all for your replies and suggestions. The problem in this study will always be the sparse, widely-distributed population. While we acquired enough detections this year to build a good detection function, in future years there won't be the time or budget to permit such intensive surveying. The original idea to combat this issue was to build a standalone detection function using this year's data and apply that function to future data.

That being said, I like the idea of pooling detections among years, so long as we can still get year-specific abundance estimates and track the population throughout time. Let's say we include year as a covariate and it is not present in the best-fit model. If this were the case, is it reasonable to calculate year-specific abundance with the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator in the manner Daniel suggested, by including year as a separate stratum and setting area for that stratum to zero? Further, could we still using stratification within years when calculating abundance for that year?

i.e:

Year     Region.Label     Area
2015     2015                 0   
2015     2015                 0   
2016     2016                 0   
2016     2016                 0   
2016     2016                 0   
2017     Stratum A        520
2017     Stratum A        520      
2017     Stratum B       1030
2017     Stratum A        520
2017     Stratum C       340

In the future, if we were to encounter a case in which year *was* included in the best-fit model, would there still be a way to obtain year-specific abundance estimates from the pooled detection function?

Thank you all for your advice. It is greatly appreciated!
